source_text: Nisi ergo necessaria possibilitas fuisset, effectus possibilis non fuisset. Ut ergo possit malum et bonum facere, necessarium est; ut autem malum faciat, non necessario, sed possibili suo debet. Ubi autem possibilitas est partis utriusque, necessitas neutra est. Sic fit ut nihil sit aliud peccatum, quam voluntas agendi quod iustitia vetat, et unde liberum est abstinere. Si nihil sit autem aliud voluntas, quam motus animi, cogente nullo, quomodo ergo Deus, ut mundum faceret, a possibili habuit; mundus autem ipse, ut existeret, a necessario pertulit; ita etiam in imagine Dei simile quiddam intellegitur. Quippe ut habeat, quam elegerit voluntatem, non cogitur; sed a possibili ei venit; illud autem quod male fecerit, ne cessitatem habet reatus. Ita crimen a necessario incurrit horrorem; licet exortum sit, non a necessitate, sed a possibilitate facientis. Opus ergo possibilitatis testimonium est liberi animantis.
pass_a_gloss: Unless therefore a necessary possibility had been, a possible effect would not have been. That he can therefore do evil and good is necessary; but that he does evil, he owes not to the necessary, but to his possible. But where there is a possibility of each part, there is neither necessity. Thus it is done that sin is nothing other than a will of doing what justice forbids, and from which it is free to abstain. But if will is nothing other than a motion of the mind, no one compelling, how therefore God, that he might make the world, had from the possible; but the world itself, that it might exist, bore from the necessary; so also in the image of God something similar is understood. For that he may have the will which he has chosen, he is not compelled; but it comes to him from the possible; but that which he shall have done evilly has a necessity of guilt. Thus a charge incurs horror from the necessary; although it arose not from necessity, but from the possibility of the one doing. The work therefore of possibility is a testimony of a free living being.

lemmas.lexica: LS necessitas; Blaise vs free choice
LS voluntas=will, wish; Blaise moral will
LS liber=free; Blaise unde liberum est abstinere
LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin

pass_b_english: Unless the capacity had existed necessarily, its possible result would not have existed. That a person can do evil and good is therefore necessary; his doing evil, however, is owed not to his necessity but to his possibility. Where either side is possible, neither is necessary. Thus sin is nothing other than the will to do what justice forbids and from which one is free to abstain. If will is nothing other than a movement of the mind under no compulsion, then just as God possessed the possibility of making the world, while the world itself received existence under necessity, so something similar is understood in God’s image. A person is not compelled to possess the will he chooses; it comes to him from possibility. The evil he has done, however, carries the necessity of guilt. Thus a crime necessarily incurs its abhorrence, although it arose not from the doer’s necessity but from his possibility. The work of possibility therefore testifies to a free living being.

choices.why: Julian's definition of sin is an act of will. Keep 'will' rather than later 'free will' system language unless liberum arbitrium is present.
Freedom to abstain is required for will and sin.
Julian's forensic/moral fault tied to will, not a substance in nature.
